Pregnancy

Taking amoxicillin during pregnancy

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Being prescribed an antibiotic during pregnancy can raise understandable questions. Amoxicillin is a penicillin antibiotic that is commonly used when a bacterial infection needs treatment. Current pregnancy-medicine guidance is reassuring about its use when recommended by a clinician; leaving a significant infection untreated can carry risks of its own.

Why it may be prescribed

Amoxicillin treats certain bacterial infections. It does not treat viruses such as a cold, and not every cough, sore throat or urinary symptom needs the same antibiotic. The prescriber considers the likely organism, the site of infection and any test results.

For a urinary infection in pregnancy, urine culture can help identify a suitable medicine. Because resistance is common in some bacteria, amoxicillin is not automatically the best treatment to start before those results are known.

A dental infection may also need a procedure to address its source. Antibiotics are not a replacement for all other treatment. Ask what the medicine is treating and when your symptoms should start improving.

Depending on the bacteria and local guidance, it may be used for selected chest, ear, throat, skin or urinary infections. It interferes with bacterial cell-wall formation. Many episodes of bronchitis are viral and do not benefit from antibiotics.

What pregnancy safety information means

Amoxicillin and other penicillins can be taken during pregnancy when a clinician recommends them. UK pregnancy-medicine guidance does not call for extra birth-defect monitoring solely because a penicillin antibiotic was used. Continue the antenatal care appropriate to your pregnancy.

Older websites may refer to FDA pregnancy category B. The FDA removed the old prescription-drug letter categories and replaced them with more detailed risk information. A letter was never a promise that a medicine had no possible risks.

The useful decision combines evidence about the medicine with the consequences of the infection and your own health. Discuss worries promptly rather than skipping doses while waiting for reassurance from an online list.

Other antibiotics, such as erythromycin or clindamycin, may sometimes be appropriate, but they are different drug classes rather than additional penicillins. Ampicillin is a penicillin. The right alternative depends on the infection and allergy history.

Share allergy and medicine information

Before taking it, tell the prescriber about previous reactions to amoxicillin, other penicillins or cephalosporins. Describe what happened and how quickly it started. An upset stomach is different from an immediate allergic reaction, but both are useful information.

A history of an antibiotic reaction needs clinical assessment; do not test the medicine yourself. The clinician may choose an alternative or clarify an inaccurate allergy label through an appropriate service.

Provide a list of prescription medicines, nonprescription treatments and supplements, and mention kidney problems. The dose, schedule and length of treatment should match your prescription rather than a general article.

Take the prescribed course correctly

Space doses as directed and follow the package instructions for your formulation. Amoxicillin can generally be taken with or without food; taking it after a meal may help if it makes you feel sick. Use a proper measuring device for liquid medicine.

If you miss a dose, follow the leaflet or ask a pharmacist. Usually it is taken when remembered unless the next dose is nearly due. Do not double doses to catch up.

Take the course for the prescribed duration unless the clinician changes the plan or a serious reaction requires stopping and urgent advice. Do not share antibiotics or save leftovers for a future illness. Resistance develops in bacteria, not because your body becomes resistant to the medicine.

Contact the prescriber if you get worse at any point or do not improve within the expected time. Do not wait until the last dose if symptoms are worsening. If vomiting makes it difficult to keep medicine down, ask what to do rather than repeatedly taking extra doses.

Recognize side effects that need help

Nausea and diarrhea can occur. Keep hydrated and ask a pharmacist or clinician before adding a diarrhea medicine, particularly during pregnancy. Report a new rash so that its significance can be assessed.

Stop the medicine and obtain emergency help for breathing difficulty, throat or tongue swelling, collapse or another severe allergic reaction. Do not take the next dose while waiting to see whether such symptoms settle.

Severe diarrhea, blood or mucus in stools, jaundice, a blistering rash or unusual bruising needs urgent medical advice. Serious diarrhea can occur during treatment or after the course; do not wait for a fixed two-day threshold if it is severe.

The next step may involve examination, tests or a change in treatment. It is not always simply another antibiotic. Bring the medicine packaging and explain that you are pregnant.

A seizure, unusual bleeding, marked weakness or fatigue, or yellow skin or eyes also warrants urgent assessment. Mild tiredness alone has many causes, but a new or severe change during treatment should be reported.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Amoxicillin can be used during pregnancy when prescribed for a suitable infection.

Take the individualized prescription correctly and seek advice for deterioration, nonresponse or significant adverse effects.

How BeMama can help

Share your allergies, medicines and pregnancy stage, then ask what improvement to expect and when to call back.

When to seek help

Severe allergic symptoms require stopping and emergency help; severe or bloody diarrhoea, jaundice, seizures or unusual bleeding needs urgent assessment.

Sources and further reading

  • UKTIS / BUMPS — Amoxicillin
  • NHS — Amoxicillin

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Amoxicillin can be used in pregnancy when appropriately prescribed.
  • The right antibiotic depends on the infection and your history.
  • Severe allergy or severe diarrhea requires prompt care.

Frequently asked questions

Does amoxicillin automatically mean extra pregnancy scans?

Not solely because of penicillin exposure, according to the pregnancy-medicine guidance reviewed. Other pregnancy or infection-related reasons may still require monitoring.

Can I stop as soon as I feel better?

Follow the prescribed duration unless your clinician changes it. Serious adverse reactions require stopping and urgent assessment rather than continuing regardless.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
